title: Usable vs. Rentable Sq Ft: Which Number Should You Quote?
seoTitle: Usable vs. Rentable Sq Ft: Which Number to Quote for Office Bids?
metaDescription: Usable vs. rentable sq ft impacts janitorial bids by 12% to 22% ($0.07-$0.15/sq ft). Compare cleanable net footage in our Office Cleaning Cost Calculator.
excerpt: Quoting your commercial lease's rentable square footage instead of actual cleanable usable footage routinely inflates annual janitorial spending by 12% to 22%. Learn how US facility managers isolate net cleanable square footage, strip out BOMA load factors, and benchmark true per-square-foot cleaning rates.
quickAnswer: Always solicit commercial janitorial quotes based on net cleanable Usable Square Footage (USF), never the Rentable Square Footage (RSF) printed on your commercial property lease. Because multi-tenant office buildings apply a 12% to 22% BOMA common-area load factor—and landlords already bill shared lobby, corridor, and core restroom upkeep through Common Area Maintenance (CAM) charges—quoting RSF causes double-billing across $0.07 to $0.15 per sq ft per visit contracts.

blocks.text: Why Lease Rentable Square Footage Distorts Janitorial Bids

When corporate real estate teams or office managers launch a Request for Proposals (RFP) for recurring janitorial services, the most frequent baseline error happens before the first vendor walkthrough: copying the square footage figure directly from the commercial lease summary. In multi-tenant Class A and Class B office buildings across the United States, leases are priced on Rentable Square Footage (RSF), governed by ANSI/BOMA Z65.1 measurement standards. RSF combines the actual private suite footprint you occupy—known as Usable Square Footage (USF)—with a pro-rata allocation of building common areas, including ground-floor marble lobbies, elevator banks, fire stairwells, mechanical rooms, and shared core restrooms.

That difference is represented by the building's R/U Ratio or Load Factor, which typically ranges from 12% in low-rise suburban office parks to 20% or 22% in high-rise downtown towers with expansive atrium lobbies. When a tenant occupies a partial floor under a triple-net (NNN) or modified gross lease, the property management firm's base building janitorial contractor cleans the common lobbies, shared corridors, and core restrooms, billing the tenant back through monthly Common Area Maintenance (CAM) reconciliations. If you hand three bidding janitorial contractors your 15,000 RSF lease figure when your suite actually contains 12,500 USF of interior carpet and tile, you are inviting vendors to price 2,500 square feet of phantom floor space that their evening crew will never touch.

blocks.title: The Net Cleanable Square Footage Rule
blocks.text: Professional janitorial estimators price labor production using Net Cleanable Square Footage—which starts with Usable Square Footage (USF) and further deducts non-serviced spaces such as locked IDF/MDF server closets, high-density mechanical vaults, and permanent wall-to-wall storage racking.
Cost Impact of Quoting RSF vs. USF vs. Net Cleanable Area

To see how measurement methodology alters contract pricing, consider a mid-sized regional headquarters occupying one partial floor in a multi-tenant commercial tower. In the 10,000 to 24,999 sq ft bracket, standard national office cleaning rates run $0.07 to $0.12 per sq ft per visit, modified by service frequency multipliers (such as 0.90x for 5x/week daily weekday service across 21.65 visits per month, calculated at 4.33 weeks per month). The table below illustrates how the exact same physical suite produces drastically different monthly invoices depending on which square footage figure governs the RFP.

blocks.text: Even at a competitive $0.081 per square foot per visit ($0.09 base rate adjusted by the 0.90 daily weekday frequency multiplier), allowing a vendor to multiply their unit price against 17,700 RSF rather than 14,400 Net Cleanable Square Feet wastes thousands of dollars annually. More importantly, it corrupts your production-rate audit: if a vendor claims they will allocate 4.5 labor hours per night based on ISSA's 3,500 sq ft/hour open-office production benchmark, an inflated RSF denominator makes an understaffed crew look adequately resourced on paper.
When You Must Quote Gross or Full-Floor Footage

There are two primary commercial occupancy scenarios where Usable Square Footage is not the final boundary of your janitorial contract, and where facility managers must intentionally expand the cleanable scope:

items: Single-Tenant Net-Lease Buildings: If your organization occupies an entire standalone flex-office or suburban headquarters building under a single-tenant triple-net lease, there is no landlord CAM crew servicing the main entrance vestibule, elevator cabs, fire stairs, or central restrooms. Your contractor must service the entire interior Gross Cleanable Area—excluding only mechanical/boiler rooms, roof hatches, and restricted electrical vaults.

Full-Floor Multi-Tenant Occupancies: Under BOMA standards, when a single tenant leases an entire floor of a multi-tenant high-rise, the elevator lobby, fire corridor loops, and core restrooms on that floor often become dedicated exclusively to that tenant. Check Section 4 or Exhibit B of your lease to confirm whether the landlord's base-building night crew services full-floor elevator lobbies and core restrooms ($15 to $30 per restroom per visit value) or if that duty transfers to the tenant's private janitorial vendor.

Private Executive Restrooms and Wet Breakrooms: Even when the building CAM crew cleans multi-stall hallway restrooms, private executive washrooms, mothers' rooms, wellness suites, and large internal cafe kitchenettes ($12 to $25 per visit add-on) located inside your suite demising walls belong strictly to your usable cleanable footprint.

blocks.text: How Flooring Density and Built-In Fixtures Modify Usable Area

Experienced commercial cleaning estimators do not view 10,000 usable square feet of wall-to-wall modular carpet tiles the same way they view 10,000 usable square feet of mixed surfaces. Once you establish the exact usable perimeter from your architectural Computer-Aided Facility Management (CAFM) drawing or CAD test-fit plan, you must break that usable square footage into surface-type zones so all bidders apply consistent production multipliers:

items: Commercial Carpet and Carpet Tiles (1.00x Baseline): Cleaned via wide-track upright or backpack HEPA vacuums at roughly 3,500 to 4,500 sq ft per labor hour depending on workstation partitioning.

VCT and LVT Vinyl Planks (1.04x Multiplier): Common in breakrooms, copy corridors, and medical-adjacent admin suites; requires dust mopping followed by neutral-pH damp mopping and periodic machine buffing.
Engineered or Solid Hardwood (1.08x Multiplier): Requires low-moisture flat microfiber pad systems with wood-safe neutral solution in executive boardrooms and reception lounges.
Ceramic Tile and Grout (1.12x Multiplier): Carries the highest floor labor load due to grout-line soil extraction, alkaline or enzymatic dwell time, and restroom-adjacent sanitation.
Polished Concrete (0.95x Multiplier): Allows rapid dust-pad and auto-scrubber passes in open creative offices with minimal chemical finish maintenance.
Mixed Carpet and Hard Surface Suites (1.05x Multiplier): Requires technicians to stage dual tool setups—both HEPA vacuum harnesses and dual-chamber mop buckets—on every evening shift.

blocks.text: Fixture density inside usable zones also dictates material handling time. For instance, placing a narrow-footprint Rubbermaid Commercial Slim Jim 23-Gallon Recycling & Waste Station (11-inch width with integrated venting channels and bag cinches) inside tight copy rooms and breakrooms reduces liner-pull drag by up to 60% compared to round cans wedged under counters. Similarly, outfitting high-traffic interior reception zones or full-floor elevator banks with a Safco Public Square 37-Gallon Commercial Steel Receptacle (fire-safe powder-coated steel with internal liner retainer) consolidates loose desk trash pulls, while an enclosed Suncast Commercial Housekeeping Cart with Locking Cabinet (300-lb capacity, 8-inch wheels, and locking chemical doors) lets day porters or evening crews traverse 15,000+ USF floors in a single pass without backtracking to the janitor closet.
Step-by-Step Protocol to Verify Net Cleanable Square Footage Before Bidding
Before releasing your janitorial RFP package, follow this four-step verification sequence to lock in an indisputable square footage baseline that every vendor must price against:

items.name: Extract Architectural CAD or As-Built Floor Plans
items.text: Request the final as-built PDF or DWG architectural floor plan from your tenant improvement (TI) architect or property manager. Unlike the lease abstract, the architectural title block lists actual interior Usable Square Footage (USF) room by room.

items.name: Deduct Non-Cleanable Security and Mechanical Exclusion Zones
items.text: Highlight all spaces where janitorial personnel are strictly prohibited from entering—such as badge-locked MDF/IDF server rooms, chemical storage vaults, high-voltage electrical closets, and leased sub-tenant cages. Subtract their exact dimensions from USF to establish Net Cleanable Square Footage.

items.name: Tag Flooring Surface Breakdowns and Wet Fixtures
items.text: List the exact square footage of carpet (1.00x), LVT/VCT (1.04x), ceramic tile (1.12x), and polished concrete (0.95x), along with exact fixture counts (toilets, urinals, sinks, breakroom appliances, and interior glass partitions at $15 to $35 per visit).

items.name: Mandate Uniform Basis of Measurement in the RFP Pricing Sheet
items.text: State in bold on your RFP bid tab: 'All per-square-foot pricing and ISSA labor hour calculations must use the verified Net Cleanable Area of X,XXX sq ft. Bids calculated on lease RSF or unverified estimates will be disqualified during technical leveling.'

faqs.q: Why does my commercial lease say 12,000 sq ft when our architect measured only 10,200 sq ft inside the suite?
faqs.a: The 12,000 sq ft figure on your lease is Rentable Square Footage (RSF), which takes your 10,200 Usable Square Feet (USF) and adds a 17.6% BOMA load factor representing your share of the building's ground lobby, mechanical rooms, fire stairs, and shared hallways. Your janitorial quote should be built strictly on the 10,200 USF figure minus any locked server closets.

faqs.q: Should we include locked server rooms and IT closets in our cleanable square footage?
faqs.a: No. Unescorted nighttime janitorial crews should never enter active MDF/IDF server rooms due to physical cybersecurity compliance, electrostatic discharge risks from standard vacuums, and trip hazards around patch cables. Exclude server closets from the base cleanable footage and schedule quarterly escorted anti-static HEPA detailing if needed.

faqs.q: How do we prevent double-paying for common-area restrooms and lobbies through both CAM and our private janitorial contract?
faqs.a: Request your landlord's Annual CAM Reconciliation and Base Building Janitorial Scope of Work. Verify that ground lobbies, shared multi-tenant corridors, and core restrooms are serviced by the property manager's vendor. Then explicitly restrict your private contractor's scope and square footage to areas inside your suite entry doors.

faqs.q: Does furniture footprint get subtracted from Usable Square Footage when calculating janitorial quotes?
faqs.a: No. Standard BOMA Usable Square Footage and ISSA 612 cleaning production rates (such as 3,500 sq ft per hour) already account for normal desk, credenza, and conference table footprints. In fact, dense furniture layouts slow down vacuuming and dusting rather than reducing work, whereas permanent floor-to-ceiling locked storage vaults are deducted.

faqs.q: How does weekly service frequency interact with usable square footage pricing?
faqs.a: Contractors multiply your net cleanable usable square footage by a per-visit rate ($0.07 to $0.12/sq ft for 10,000–24,999 sq ft offices), adjust for frequency (1.08x for 1x/week, 1.00x for 2x/week, or 0.90x for 5x/week daily service), and multiply by exact monthly visits using 4.33 weeks per month (21.65 visits/month for 5x/week).
